title: How to embrace curiosity as a superpower
text:
How to embrace curiosity as a superpower
What fifteen years and a doctorate taught me about changing people's minds
In high school I made a name for myself, in my various little social circles, for debating. Political issues, mostly, which made me exactly the fan favorite you’re imagining at lunch, at soccer practice, or the occasional soiree. I was good at it. I could take a position, ask a seemingly innocent question and then spring the trap to secure my victory. I was also, with the full benefit of hindsight, a self-righteous little prick.
What took me far too long to realize (and what I still sometimes forget) is that winning an argument and genuinely helping a person are two entirely different things. I’ve ‘won’ plenty of arguments. And people would nod, and go on with their life unchanged. Sometimes it was worse. I’d win, feel the room cool, and realize that I’d made my case and lost a little of the person and my relationship with them in the process.
I was right. And I was not helpful.
Fast forward a number of years, and I was deep into my doctorate to ask the question: what makes a person change? I was interested for science (yay science!) and as a student of my own perplexing behavior. Why wouldn’t I go to the gym when I said I needed to? Why couldn’t I make myself get up in the morning? Why wasn’t as I kind as I knew I could be? I Going into the PhD, I was certain I knew the answer: better data, better logic, just understand more. Surely, if you just give people information and present a convincing case, that would be good enough.
I could not have been more wrong. Telling someone the ‘truth’ (or at least, your version of it) does not work.
William Miller and Stephen Rollnick, who built motivational interviewing out of thirty years of addiction work, call this the righting reflex: the itch to fix, to correct, to hand over the answer. It backfires almost every time. The moment you argue for someone’s change, they start arguing against it, instinctively, and out loud. Nobody enjoys an external force, or judge in this case, laying out all the ways in which they haven’t changed yet. What my many (many) pages of reading of academic research left me with is that we are most persuaded by what we hear ourselves say. Not by what gets told to us or spoken at us. Meaning my powers of debate and persuasion made me ineffective and an asshole. A two for one sale!
You cannot talk anyone into their own life. The answer is instead to ask better questions. As my new friend, Julia, writes:
“Because, after all, who does not like to be listened to?”
Not all questions are created equal. You can include a question mark to disguise a true purpose of steering someone towards your answer. That’s called lawyering, others can feel it, and it sucks. You can also give advice disguised as a question, “Have you tried…” or “Do you think…” Not real questions and not true curiosity.
Enter Joe Hudson, who coaches executives at Apple and OpenAI. His principle about questions is ask them with a sense of wonder. Wonder is curiosity without any idea what the answer might be. Instead of chasing an answer that might tighten the recipient as if they’re being tested in front of the class (because sometimes that’s exactly what you’re doing), wonder stays open. Look at the clouds and tell me, what do you see? There’s no right answer and that’s the beginning of a conversation that strengthens a relationship.
The opposite of wonder is certainty. I am certain this is the thing you should do next. I know exactly what it’s like to be in your shoes. I will ask this question to appear like I know what I’m doing.
Don’t do that. Be curious instead.
Researcher and professor Todd Kashdan spent his career on this concept. In Curious? he says:
“Curiosity creates possibilities; the need for certainty narrows them. Curiosity creates energy; the need for certainty depletes. Curiosity results in exploration; the need for certainty creates closure. Curiosity creates movement; the need for certainty is about replaying events. Curiosity creates relationships; the need for certainty creates defensiveness. Curiosity is about discovery; the need for certainty is about being right.”
Curiosity creates relationships; the need for certainty creates defensiveness. Every person I know who is certain about everything is also, quietly, a person nobody seeks out and nobody listens to. In other words, they are an ass.
The two corrections
Wonder is a disposition towards the world and towards others. Wonder in curiosity says “I have no fkn idea what you might say to this. Isn’t that magical?” There are a couple of ways to action this:
Ask what instead of why. “Why did you do that” puts a person on trial. It implies there was another, better way of doing something and the subject of your interrogation will find themselves scrambling for a reason to get away. That does not create closeness. Don’t make them justify their actions, invite them to explain their thought process. Instead, “What were you hoping for” opens a door to an answer that you genuinely could not know what they might say next.This part is crucial. After you ask your question… shut tf up. Silence from you. For as long as it takes for them to answer. Your job is to sit quiet enough, not fill the space, no matter how awkward, to allow someone the space to think. This is a gift you can give to people in your life, genuine care to give them breathing room in a world of distraction.
At work
I spend most of my days working with leaders on leading like a coach, meaning you need to ask more than you tell. It feels weird, possibly wrong, for most because many of us got promoted and advanced for having all the answers. But in your leadership journey, especially as you move up, your people don’t need you to have all the answers as much as they need you to empower them to go find them. If you stop thinking for them, you stop being a bottleneck for every decision and you return power back, like the hero Bane in Dark Knight Rises, “to the people.” How nice of you.
If you need a starting point, I give leaders three questions to ask in a sequence that can take fifteen minutes or an hour:
A genuine “How are you doing?”
In the next 6-12 months, what do you want?
How can I help?
People will feel if these questions are asked with authenticity or if you’re just going through the motions. And they will appreciate the time and space you create you sit to hear them.
At home
In 1997, Arthur Aron ran a study taking different pairings of two complete strangers, had them ask a series thirty-six questions that escalate in emotional intensity in forty-five minutes. And in less than hour, just through questions, these people reported feeling a greater sense of intimacy, defined as “a process in which each feels his or her innermost self validated, understood, and cared for by the other.” By a stranger. Someone they’d never met ever. In 45 minutes.
How many people in your life truly validate, understand, and care for you? Most of us are lucky if we can even say one. Some of us may not be able to say that. What this study revealed is that closeness can occur by virtue of time, but it does not have to be about years accumulated. It can be about the questions we ask and the space we give to know a person. And unfortunately, in many of our closest relationships, the ones we say we’d take a bullet for, we stop asking the genuine, curious questions. Subconsciously, we file someone under “I know you” and move on.
The same fix-reflex that won me all those arguments back in the day shows up sneaky in my everyday life. It looks a lot like someone you love says they’re struggling and every cell in your body lunges to solve it. I will help by Fixing the job. Fixing the mood. Fixing the kid. It’s usually not what people want. And it’s not my job to fix. It’s my job to get curious. “What will be most useful right now? What do you need from me? Tell me more.” Such remarkably simple language and seemingly so difficult to remember to ask.
This idea is a skill I teach to adults in business as they step into leadership roles.
A) It is a fun thing to bring online for others as you get to walk around metaphorically smacking their wrist as they ask questions designed to gather information/advice giving in disguise. It’s a new muscle for many of us when we were trained to fix and solve problems but it is learnable.
B) It is one of the most satisfying parts of my job to hear where and how people start to deploy this concept. It’s great to hear about how it helps them and their teams at work, it fills my heart with joy to hear about how it works at home.
I worked with a badass single mom whose whole role at work had her keeping everyone in line, managing difficult personalities up, sideways, and down throughout the org. Her role was rescue and she was damn good at it. And as a single parent, she played the same role at home. One of the kids had a problem, she solved it, everyone exhaled, repeat. And one day, near the close of our program, she came to me to say, “these questions changed my life.” Her son came to her stuck on something, and she felt the answer forming in her mouth before he’d even finished his sentence. And instead of rescuing, instead of fixing, she asked him a question, “What do you think you should do?” And then she was quiet. And her son, this beautiful human she had brought into the world and would do anything for, started working the problem out loud in front of her. She didn’t have to fix. She didn’t have to rescue. She just needed to create space. Two weeks later she told me she'd stopped answering half the questions her team brought her, empowering and trusting them to find the right answers, saving her time and giving them agency. Win-win-win.
Note: asking more curious questions does not mean abandoning people to run willy-nilly in any direction in service of chaos and disorder. At work or at home, there are still guardrails to follow. The trick is to try and ask questions first of the person before jumping in with corrections, nudges, or genuine solutions that might be helpful to them. It’s learning to let others do more of the work before you swing in with a superhero cape.
I don’t win many arguments anymore. I’ve mostly lost the taste for it. “I don’t know” and “I don’t have an opinion” keep me out of trouble. When I land in a sticky disagreement and manage to catch myself, I remember my job, first and foremost, is to ask and learn where the other person is coming from. That’s it.
Not long ago my brother and I had a disagreement. Nothing serious. He gave me some advice I did not want and did not ask for and I felt some type of way about that. And very quickly, as is oft the case with siblings, it was time to squabble up. We fell into the same grooves worn deep over years of little tiffs and bickering. He’s my best friend in the world and he drives me utterly insane sometimes (luv ya bud). But in the midst of this I felt all the old reflexes warming up. Time to assemble the arguments, spring a trap, close the case, and win the day. The siren song of “debate and win” and therefore fix this sought to tempt me onto its shores. Instead, I said let's save solutions, the only win tonight is to leave understanding each other a little better than we do right now. Within a few minutes, with neither of us trying to win, the whole thing came apart. We left with our relationship in a better place.
The batting average on this is absurd. Drop the need to win, aim only at understanding, and the problem has a habit of solving itself. It’s quite pleasant.
You can’t talk anyone into their own life. Not your team, not your partner. This week, take one hard conversation and walk in with a single goal: understand, not solve. Ask one real question. Then shut up, long enough to be surprised. Stay in curiosity, wonder, and the question. That’s where the real answer lives.
I made a version of this article with pretty pictures, if you’d rather watch than read: dkenny.net/talks/curiosity.
And if you want to get deliberate about this, with your team or on your own, that’s the work I do: coaching for individuals, facilitation for organizations. You can always just hit reply.
